nameStory: This ancient-looking plant gets its common name from its resemblance to a tiny evergreen tree topped with a club-like structure. The species name 'hickeyi' honors botanist Lewis Hickey, who studied these fascinating prehistoric plants. It's also called Pennsylvania clubmoss, reflecting one of the states where it's commonly found.
description: Hickey's tree-clubmoss is a low-growing, evergreen plant that looks like a miniature pine tree, typically reaching 6-12 inches tall. Despite its tree-like appearance, it's not actually a tree or moss at all, but rather an ancient type of plant more closely related to ferns. The plant has a main upright stem that branches into several smaller, tree-like sections with tiny needle-like leaves arranged in spirals around the stems. In summer, it produces distinctive club-shaped spore cones at the tips of some branches.

idTips.label: Tree-like branching pattern
idTips.description: Multiple upright stems branch out like tiny evergreen trees, each 4-8 inches tall with a distinct main trunk and side branches

idTips.label: Needle-like leaves
idTips.description: Tiny, scale-like leaves spiral around the stems, feeling soft and slightly fuzzy to the touch, much smaller than pine needles

idTips.label: Club-shaped spore cones
idTips.description: Yellow to tan cylindrical structures about 1-2 inches long appear at branch tips in summer, releasing a cloud of yellow spores when disturbed

idTips.label: Colonial growth habit
idTips.description: Often forms patches or colonies of multiple plant clusters connected by underground runners, creating carpets in suitable habitat

idTips.label: Evergreen appearance
idTips.description: Remains green year-round with a fresh, slightly resinous scent when crushed, similar to but milder than pine

habitat: Hickey's tree-clubmoss thrives in acidic, well-drained soils of mixed and coniferous forests throughout New England. Look for it in partial shade under pines, hemlocks, and oaks, often on slopes or woodland edges where the soil stays moist but not waterlogged. It's particularly common in areas with sandy or rocky soil and can be found from sea level to moderate elevations in the mountains.

seasonality.spring: New growth begins to emerge, with fresh green shoots extending from the previous year's growth, making the colonies appear brighter and more vigorous.
seasonality.summer: Peak identification season when distinctive club-shaped spore cones appear at branch tips, releasing clouds of yellow spores when mature and disturbed.
seasonality.fall: Spore cones turn brown and dry out, but the evergreen foliage remains bright green and easily visible as deciduous leaves fall around it.
seasonality.winter: Remains evergreen and identifiable under snow, though may appear slightly dulled; often the only green plant visible on the forest floor.

funFact: This little plant is a living fossil that has remained virtually unchanged for over 300 million years, meaning it was already ancient when the first dinosaurs appeared and survived multiple mass extinctions that wiped out countless other species!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with its close relatives flat-branched tree-clubmoss and prickly tree-clubmoss, which grow in similar habitats. Hickey's tends to have more open, less dense branching than prickly tree-clubmoss, and its branches are more three-dimensional rather than the flattened, fan-like appearance of flat-branched tree-clubmoss. Memory trick: Hickey's has a more 'relaxed' branching pattern compared to its bushier cousins.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'moss,' clubmosses are not true mosses at all but belong to an ancient group of plants that reproduce by spores rather than seeds. The classification of tree-clubmosses has been debated by botanists, with some placing them in the genus Lycopodium and others in the separate genus Dendrolycopodium, which is why you might see both names in field guides.
compareHints: Hickey's tree-clubmoss differs from flat-branched tree-clubmoss by having more three-dimensional, upright branching rather than flattened, fan-like branches. Compared to prickly tree-clubmoss, Hickey's has a more open, less densely packed appearance with branches that spread out more loosely. All three species can grow together, but Hickey's tends to have the most 'tree-like' proportions with clearly defined main stems and side branches.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Flat-branched tree-clubmoss stands out from its relatives by its distinctly flattened, fan-like branching pattern - prickly tree-clubmoss has more rounded, bottle-brush-like branches, while Hickey's tree-clubmoss tends to be more upright and less flattened.
Prickly tree-clubmoss differs from flat-branched tree-clubmoss by having round (not flattened) side shoots and all leaves the same size, while flat-branched has different sized leaves.
